questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with 15 years of GERD undergoes surveillance endoscopy. Biopsies from the distal esophagus show that the normal stratified squamous epithelium has been replaced by columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Which term best describes this finding, and what is its significance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reflux esophagitis; the most common acute complication of GERD

choices.label: B
choices.text: Barrett esophagus; a premalignant intestinal metaplasia predisposing to adenocarcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eosinophilic esophagitis; an allergen-driven inflammatory disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous dysplasia; a precursor to squamous cell carcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peptic stricture; a fibrotic narrowing from chronic acid injury

explanation.summary: Columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing squamous epithelium defines Barrett esophagus, a premalignant metaplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia in which squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells; it is premalignant and raises adenocarcinoma risk roughly 30-fold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reflux esophagitis shows basal cell hyperplasia and inflammation of squamous epithelium, not columnar metaplasia with goblet cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eosinophilic esophagitis shows numerous intraepithelial eosinophils in squamous mucosa, not goblet-cell metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Squamous dysplasia involves atypia of squamous epithelium, whereas this is columnar (glandular) metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A peptic stricture is a fibrotic luminal narrowing, a gross/structural change, not a histologic metaplasia.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with chronic heartburn undergoes endoscopy with distal esophageal biopsy. There is no columnar metaplasia. Histology shows thickening of the basal cell layer and elongation of the lamina propria papillae toward the epithelial surface, with scattered intraepithelial inflammatory cells. Which condition do these findings represent?

explanation.summary: Basal cell hyperplasia with elongated papillae and intraepithelial inflammation is the histologic hallmark of reflux esophagitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reflux esophagitis shows basal cell layer hyperplasia, elongation of lamina propria papillae, and intraepithelial inflammatory cells as an injury response to acid, without columnar metaplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Barrett esophagus requires intestinal (columnar) metaplasia with goblet cells, which is explicitly absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophilic esophagitis is defined by ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field, which is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CMV esophagitis shows enlarged cells with intranuclear 'owl's eye' inclusions in ulcer bases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV esophagitis shows multinucleated giant cells with Cowdry type A inclusions at ulcer margins.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with erosive reflux esophagitis is prescribed omeprazole. To maximize efficacy, she should take it about 30 minutes before a meal. Which action best describes this drug's mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neutralizes existing gastric acid with an alkaline base

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitively blocks the histamine H2 receptor on parietal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forms a viscous barrier that adheres to ulcerated mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversibly inhibits the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase, the final step of acid secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulates prostaglandin production to enhance mucosal defense

explanation.summary: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+ ATPase, the final common step in acid secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly inhibits the parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase, blocking the final step of acid production; taking it before a meal targets actively secreting pumps.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neutralizing acid with an alkaline base describes antacids, not PPIs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking the H2 receptor describes H2 receptor antagonists such as famotidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Forming a protective mucosal barrier describes sucralfate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enhancing prostaglandin-mediated mucosal defense describes misoprostol.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman reports intermittent difficulty swallowing solids. Labs show a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with low ferritin. Barium swallow demonstrates a thin, eccentric membrane in the proximal (cervical) esophagus. This constellation places her at increased risk for which malignancy?

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anemia plus a proximal esophageal web is Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which raises squamous cell carcinoma risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The triad of iron deficiency anemia, a post-cricoid (proximal) esophageal web, and dysphagia defines Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which carries an increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenocarcinoma is the malignancy associated with Barrett esophagus/GERD, not with proximal webs and iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric adenocarcinoma is not the malignancy linked to Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MALT lymphoma is associated with chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis, not esophageal webs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GIST is a mesenchymal tumor unrelated to esophageal webs or iron deficiency.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man reports episodes of solid food, especially steak and bread, momentarily lodging in his lower chest, relieved by drinking water or regurgitating the bolus. Between episodes he swallows normally, and he has no weight loss. Endoscopy reveals a thin circumferential mucosal ring at the gastroesophageal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A thin circumferential ring at the GE junction causing intermittent solid dysphagia ('steakhouse syndrome') is a Schatzki ring.
explanation.whyCorrect: A Schatzki ring is a thin mucosal ring at the GE junction that causes intermittent solid-food dysphagia, classically with meat and bread ('steakhouse syndrome'), with normal swallowing between episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A peptic stricture causes progressive (not intermittent) solid dysphagia and appears as a smooth tapered narrowing, not a thin ring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids with impaired LES relaxation, not intermittent solid-only episodes from a ring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diffuse esophageal spasm causes chest pain and intermittent dysphagia due to disordered contractions, without a mucosal ring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zenker diverticulum causes regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis from a proximal pouch, not a distal ring.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has severe GERD refractory to maximal PPI therapy and lifestyle modification, with a large sliding hiatal hernia. He is offered a surgical procedure that wraps the gastric fundus 360 degrees around the distal esophagus to reinforce the antireflux barrier. Which procedure is this?

explanation.summary: Nissen fundoplication wraps the fundus 360 degrees around the distal esophagus for refractory GERD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication wraps the gastric fundus 360 degrees around the distal esophagus and repairs any hiatal hernia to strengthen the antireflux barrier, used for GERD refractory to medical therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cricopharyngeal myotomy treats Zenker diverticulum/cricopharyngeal dysfunction, not GERD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heller myotomy divides the LES muscle to treat achalasia, the opposite goal of reinforcing the sphincter.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Esophagectomy is resection of the esophagus, used for malignancy or high-grade dysplasia, not routine GERD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumatic dilation stretches/disrupts the LES for achalasia and would worsen reflux rather than treat it.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 39-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 3 months ago develops severe odynophagia. Endoscopy shows large, deep, linear ulcers in the distal esophagus. Biopsy of the ulcer base reveals enlarged cells with intranuclear 'owl's eye' inclusions and cytoplasmic inclusions. Which organism is responsible?

explanation.summary: Large linear ulcers with 'owl's eye' intranuclear inclusions identify CMV esophagitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: CMV esophagitis in immunocompromised patients produces large, deep, linear ulcers, and biopsy of the ulcer base shows enlarged cells with intranuclear 'owl's eye' and cytoplasmic inclusions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida causes white plaques with pseudohyphae, not deep linear ulcers with viral inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV causes small punched-out ulcers with Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions and multinucleated giant cells sampled from the ulcer margin, not owl's eye inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: EBV is not a typical cause of infectious esophagitis with these inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV is associated with squamous papillomas, not owl's-eye inclusion ulcers.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is found on CT to have a portion of stomach herniated into the thorax alongside the esophagus, while the gastroesophageal junction remains in its normal intra-abdominal position. She has minimal reflux symptoms. Compared with a sliding hiatal hernia, this hernia type is most notable for which feature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strong association with severe acid reflux

choices.label: B
choices.text: Displacement of the GE junction into the chest

choices.label: C
choices.text: Being the most common type of hiatal hernia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Risk of gastric volvulus and strangulation

explanation.summary: A paraesophageal hernia keeps the GE junction in place but risks gastric volvulus/strangulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a paraesophageal hernia the GE junction stays intra-abdominal, so reflux is usually not prominent; its major concern is that the herniated stomach can twist (gastric volvulus) and strangulate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: With the GE junction in normal position, paraesophageal hernias are generally not associated with significant reflux.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Displacement of the GE junction into the chest characterizes a sliding hernia, not a paraesophageal one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sliding hernias, not paraesophageal, are the most common type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Barrett esophagus results from chronic acid reflux; a paraesophageal hernia with minimal reflux does not directly progress to it.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department after an episode of violent vomiting following a large meal and heavy drinking. He now has severe, sudden retrosternal and epigastric pain, is febrile and tachycardic, and appears toxic. Exam reveals crepitus over the chest wall. Chest imaging shows pneumomediastinum and a left pleural effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peptic ulcer perforation into the peritoneum

explanation.summary: Full-thickness esophageal rupture after vomiting with pneumomediastinum and sepsis is Boerhaave syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Boerhaave syndrome is a spontaneous full-thickness esophageal rupture from forceful vomiting; leakage into the mediastinum causes chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus), pneumomediastinum, effusion, and sepsis, and requires urgent surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A Mallory-Weiss tear is mucosal only, presenting with hematemesis in a stable patient, not pneumomediastinum and sepsis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myocardial infarction does not produce pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous crepitus, or a vomiting-triggered esophageal leak.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptic ulcer perforation causes free peritoneal air and peritonitis, not pneumomediastinum after vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aortic dissection causes tearing pain and mediastinal widening but not pneumomediastinum from esophageal contents.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with asthma and seasonal allergies reports several years of intermittent solid-food dysphagia and one episode of food impaction requiring endoscopic removal. He does not respond to acid suppression. Endoscopy shows concentric rings and linear furrows, and biopsies reveal 25 eosinophils per high-power field. Which is the most appropriate description of this disorder and its management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An acid-mediated disorder best treated with lifelong high-dose antacids alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chronic immune/antigen-mediated disorder managed with swallowed topical steroids, dietary elimination, and dilation for strictures

choices.label: C
choices.text: A premalignant metaplasia requiring endoscopic ablation

choices.label: D
choices.text: An infectious process treated with fluconazole

choices.label: E
choices.text: A motility disorder treated with pneumatic dilation of the LES

explanation.summary: Rings, furrows, and ≥15 eos/HPF in an atopic young man indicate eosinophilic esophagitis, treated with the '3 Ds.'
explanation.whyCorrect: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic Th2 immune/antigen-mediated disorder (≥15 eosinophils/HPF) in atopic patients; management uses the '3 Ds': Drugs (PPIs, swallowed topical steroids), Diet (food elimination), and Dilation for strictures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EoE is not primarily acid-mediated, and antacids alone are inadequate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is inflammatory, not a premalignant columnar metaplasia like Barrett esophagus requiring ablation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no infection; eosinophilic infiltration, not fungal elements, is present, so antifungals are inappropriate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: EoE is not an LES motility disorder; pneumatic dilation treats achalasia, not EoE.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with osteoporosis develops sudden retrosternal pain and odynophagia the morning after taking her weekly alendronate tablet with a small sip of water at bedtime. Endoscopy shows a discrete, localized ulcer in the mid-esophagus at the level of the aortic arch, with surrounding normal mucosa. Which intervention would most likely have prevented this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Starting a proton pump inhibitor before the tablet

choices.label: E
choices.text: Taking the pill upright with a full glass of water and remaining upright afterward

explanation.summary: Pill esophagitis is prevented by taking pills upright with adequate water and staying upright.
explanation.whyCorrect: A localized ulcer at an anatomic narrowing after a bedtime bisphosphonate with little water is pill esophagitis; taking the pill upright with a full glass of water and remaining upright prevents the tablet from lodging and injuring the mucosa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A PPI treats acid-mediated reflux injury but does not prevent direct caustic injury from a lodged pill.
whyWrongByChoice.B: H. pylori causes gastroduodenal disease, not a discrete pill-induced esophageal ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no fungal infection; antifungal prophylaxis is irrelevant to pill esophagitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dietary acid triggers relate to GERD symptoms, not to a mechanically lodged tablet causing focal injury.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man undergoing chemotherapy for leukemia develops acute odynophagia. Endoscopy reveals multiple small, discrete, 'punched-out' ulcers with raised edges in the mid-esophagus. Biopsy taken from the ulcer margin shows multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic intranuclear (Cowdry type A) inclusions. Which organism is the cause?

explanation.summary: Punched-out ulcers with Cowdry type A inclusions and multinucleated giant cells indicate HSV esophagitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV esophagitis produces small, discrete punched-out ulcers; biopsy of the ulcer margin shows multinucleated giant cells with Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV causes large linear ulcers with 'owl's eye' intranuclear inclusions in cells at the ulcer base, not Cowdry type A inclusions in giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Candida produces adherent white plaques with pseudohyphae, not punched-out ulcers with viral inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tuberculous esophagitis is rare and does not show Cowdry type A inclusions or giant multinucleated epithelial cells of viral type.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV is associated with squamous papillomas, not ulcerative inclusion-bearing lesions.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A gastroenterologist is counseling a patient with long-standing GERD about the natural history of Barrett esophagus. Approximately what proportion of GERD patients develop Barrett esophagus, and by roughly how much does Barrett esophagus increase the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 50% of GERD patients; roughly 2-fold increased risk

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1% of GERD patients; roughly 100-fold increased risk

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 5–15% of GERD patients; roughly 30-fold increased risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 25% of GERD patients; no meaningful increase in risk

choices.label: E
choices.text: Essentially 0%; Barrett esophagus is unrelated to GERD

explanation.summary: About 5–15% of GERD patients develop Barrett esophagus, raising adenocarcinoma risk roughly 30-fold.
explanation.whyCorrect: Roughly 5–15% of GERD patients develop Barrett esophagus, and this intestinal metaplasia increases esophageal adenocarcinoma risk about 30-fold, justifying surveillance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Barrett develops in a minority of GERD patients and the cancer risk increase is far greater than 2-fold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The prevalence is higher than 1% and the risk increase, while substantial, is on the order of 30-fold, not 100-fold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The prevalence figure is too high, and Barrett esophagus clearly does increase adenocarcinoma risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Barrett esophagus is a direct consequence of chronic GERD, not unrelated to it.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A physiology instructor is describing the components of the antireflux barrier at the gastroesophageal junction. In addition to the tonic pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter and the external compression provided by the crural diaphragm, which anatomic feature acts as a flap valve that helps prevent reflux?

explanation.summary: The angle of His acts as a flap valve completing the three-component antireflux barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The antireflux barrier has three components: the LES, the crural diaphragm as an external sphincter, and the acute angle of His between the gastric cardia and esophagus, which functions as a flap valve to prevent reflux.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The phrenoesophageal membrane anchors the GE junction at the hiatus but is not the flap-valve component of the antireflux barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Z-line marks the squamocolumnar mucosal transition and has no valve function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The cricopharyngeus is the upper esophageal sphincter and does not act as the lower flap valve against reflux.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The incisura angularis is a gastric landmark on the lesser curvature, unrelated to the antireflux flap valve.

questions.topicName: Benign Esophageal Disorders: GERD, Esophagitis, and Structural Disorders
questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with worsening GERD is found on endoscopy to have upward displacement of the gastroesophageal junction and gastric cardia through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax. Which mechanism best explains how this anatomic change promotes reflux?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases the resting tone of the lower esophageal sphincter

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reduces the frequency of transient LES relaxations

choices.label: C
choices.text: It sharpens the angle of His, strengthening the flap valve

choices.label: D
choices.text: It displaces the LES into the chest, separating it from the crural diaphragm and exposing it to negative intrathoracic pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: It accelerates gastric emptying, reducing gastric distention

explanation.summary: A sliding hiatal hernia moves the LES into the thorax, uncoupling it from the crural diaphragm and exposing it to negative intrathoracic pressure that favors reflux.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a sliding hiatal hernia the GE junction and LES are displaced above the diaphragm, separating the LES from the reinforcing crural diaphragm and exposing it to negative intrathoracic pressure, which favors reflux.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A sliding hernia weakens, not increases, the effective antireflux pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It does not decrease TLESRs; if anything, herniation is associated with more reflux, not less.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herniation flattens (blunts) the angle of His, impairing the flap valve rather than strengthening it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A hiatal hernia does not accelerate gastric emptying, and faster emptying would not be the mechanism of reflux here.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a nonhealing ulcer on the lateral tongue for 3 months, with pain on chewing and occasional bleeding. He has chewed tobacco daily for 30 years and drinks alcohol. Exam shows an ulcerated lesion with irregular, raised, indurated borders. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: An indurated, nonhealing oral ulcer in a tobacco/alcohol user is squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 95% of head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas, and oral cavity SCC is strongly associated with tobacco and alcohol use. Chewing tobacco is particularly linked to SCC of the buccal mucosa, gingiva, and tongue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pleomorphic adenoma is a benign salivary gland tumor presenting as a painless parotid mass, not an ulcerated mucosal lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Warthin tumor is a benign salivary (parotid) tumor, not a tongue ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenocarcinoma of this region is not the typical oral mucosal malignancy; SCC dominates the oral cavity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is a salivary gland malignancy, not the classic tobacco-related tongue ulcer.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a painless neck mass and no other symptoms. Excisional biopsy of a cervical node shows nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma with nests of basaloid cells among sheets of lymphocytes, and the tumor stains strongly for p16. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prior radiation to the salivary glands

explanation.summary: p16-positive, nonkeratinizing SCC presenting as an asymptomatic neck mass is HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oropharyngeal SCC is now caused primarily by high-risk HPV, particularly HPV16. It is nonkeratinizing, p16 positive, and classically presents as an asymptomatic neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy from a small primary tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic reflux causes Barrett esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma, not p16-positive oropharyngeal SCC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Smokeless tobacco drives keratinizing oral cavity SCC (p16 negative), not this nonkeratinizing p16-positive pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency with webs (Plummer-Vinson) is a risk for esophageal SCC, not p16-positive oropharyngeal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salivary gland radiation is a risk for salivary neoplasms, not HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a slowly enlarging, painless, mobile mass near the angle of the jaw. It is resected, and histology shows a well-demarcated tumor with epithelial and myoepithelial cells set in a chondromyxoid matrix containing islands of cartilage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Epithelial/myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid matrix define pleomorphic adenoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary gland neoplasm (~60% of parotid tumors). It is a benign mixed tumor with epithelial and myoepithelial cells embedded in a chondromyxoid (cartilage-like) stroma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Warthin tumor shows double-layered oncocytic epithelium over lymphoid stroma, not a chondromyxoid matrix.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is composed of mucous, squamous, and intermediate cells, not a chondromyxoid stroma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenoid cystic carcinoma shows cribriform 'Swiss cheese' nests with perineural invasion, not chondromyxoid matrix.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Squamous cell carcinoma shows malignant keratinocytes, not a benign mixed chondromyxoid tumor.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 43-year-old man who smokes presents with a mobile, painless mass in the tail of the parotid gland. Resection reveals a tumor composed of a double layer of oncocytic epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm overlying a lymphoid stroma with germinal centers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Oncocytic cells in a double layer over lymphoid stroma with germinal centers, in a smoker, is Warthin tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Warthin tumor is the second most common salivary gland neoplasm, arises almost exclusively in the parotid, and is strongly associated with smoking. It is characterized by oncocytic (mitochondria-rich) epithelium over lymphoid stroma with germinal centers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pleomorphic adenoma shows epithelial/myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid matrix, not oncocytic cells over lymphoid stroma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma has mucous, squamous, and intermediate cells, not oncocytic/lymphoid architecture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Squamous cell carcinoma shows malignant keratinocytes, not a benign oncocytic tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenoid cystic carcinoma shows cribriform nests with perineural spread, not oncocytic cells over lymphoid stroma.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux develops progressive solid-food dysphagia and weight loss. Endoscopy shows a mass in the distal esophagus, and biopsy reveals malignant glands arising in a background of intestinal metaplasia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the upper esophagus

explanation.summary: Distal esophageal malignant glands on a background of intestinal metaplasia (Barrett) is adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Esophageal adenocarcinoma is the most common esophageal cancer in the Western world. It arises in the distal third of the esophagus from Barrett esophagus (intestinal metaplasia) driven by chronic GERD, and shows malignant glandular histology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Esophageal SCC arises in the upper two thirds and shows squamous, not glandular, histology; it is not linked to Barrett.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Small cell carcinoma of the esophagus is rare and shows small round blue cells, not malignant glands from metaplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leiomyosarcoma is a mesenchymal (smooth muscle) tumor, not a glandular epithelial malignancy from Barrett.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is a salivary gland malignancy, not the expected Barrett-associated esophageal cancer.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man from a region where esophageal cancer is endemic presents with dysphagia. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and drinks alcohol heavily. Endoscopy shows a stricturing mass in the mid-esophagus, and biopsy shows malignant nests of squamous epithelium without a Barrett background. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for this cancer?

explanation.summary: Mid-esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is driven primarily by smoking and alcohol.
explanation.whyCorrect: Esophageal SCC arises in the upper two thirds of the esophagus and is the most common esophageal cancer worldwide. Smoking is the most significant risk factor, along with alcohol, hot liquids, caustic injury, and Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic reflux drives distal adenocarcinoma via Barrett esophagus, not mid-esophageal SCC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HPV16 is the major driver of oropharyngeal SCC, not the classic esophageal SCC in this vignette.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Obesity (via reflux) is associated with adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Barrett esophagus is the precursor to adenocarcinoma; this SCC arose without a Barrett background.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has a keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the floor of the mouth. Imaging shows a locally advanced primary tumor with ipsilateral cervical lymph nodes but no distant metastases. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Observation with repeat imaging in 6 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Surgical resection with possible adjuvant radiation therapy

explanation.summary: Oral cavity SCC management centers on surgical resection with possible adjuvant radiation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of oral cavity neoplasms is primarily surgical resection of the primary tumor and involved nodes, with adjuvant radiation therapy for advanced or high-risk disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Observation is inappropriate for a locally advanced invasive cancer that requires definitive treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticosteroids do not treat squamous cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no antiviral therapy that treats established SCC, and this keratinizing oral cavity tumor is not HPV-driven.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PPIs address reflux/Barrett, not oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a newly biopsy-proven oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma needs staging before treatment. Which of the following imaging studies is most appropriate to assess the extent of locoregional and metastatic disease?

choices.label: C
choices.text: CT of the neck and chest with contrast

explanation.summary: CT of the neck and chest with contrast is the preferred staging study for oral cavity neoplasms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest evaluates the primary tumor extent, regional nodal drainage, and thoracic metastatic spread, making it the preferred staging modality.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A plain mandible radiograph cannot adequately assess soft tissue extent, nodes, or metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abdominal ultrasound does not evaluate the relevant head, neck, and chest disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Brain PET is not the routine staging study; the neck and chest are the priority sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A barium swallow evaluates luminal contour but does not stage nodal or metastatic disease.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A pathologist reviews two oral squamous cell carcinomas. Tumor 1 shows nests of basaloid cells within sheets of lymphocytes and stains strongly for p16. Tumor 2 shows malignant keratinocytes forming keratin whorls that invade stroma and muscle. Which statement best distinguishes these two tumors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tumor 1 is keratinizing and tobacco-related; Tumor 2 is HPV-associated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both tumors are p16 positive and HPV-driven

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor 1 is HPV-associated nonkeratinizing SCC; Tumor 2 is non-HPV keratinizing SCC

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor 1 typically presents with a large primary tumor and severe odynophagia

explanation.summary: Nonkeratinizing p16-positive SCC is HPV-associated; keratinizing p16-negative SCC is tobacco/alcohol-related.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor 1 (nonkeratinizing, basaloid nests among lymphocytes, p16 positive) is HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC. Tumor 2 (keratinizing with keratin whorls) is the non-HPV, tobacco/alcohol-related pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the two: the p16-positive nonkeratinizing tumor is HPV-related, and the keratinizing one is tobacco-related.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only Tumor 1 is p16 positive and HPV-driven; the keratinizing tumor is not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Barrett metaplasia gives rise to esophageal adenocarcinoma, not an oral keratinizing SCC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV-associated SCC typically presents with a small primary and an asymptomatic neck mass, not a large tumor with severe odynophagia.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a firm parotid mass that is resected and diagnosed as mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Which of the following best describes this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A benign tumor with a chondromyxoid matrix

choices.label: B
choices.text: A benign oncocytic tumor with lymphoid stroma

choices.label: C
choices.text: A cancer arising from Barrett esophagus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The most common primary malignant tumor of the salivary glands, composed of mucous, squamous, and intermediate cells

explanation.summary: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common salivary gland malignancy, with mucous, squamous, and intermediate cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common primary malignant salivary gland tumor (~15% of all salivary tumors), most often in the parotid, and is composed of mucous, squamous (epidermoid), and intermediate cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chondromyxoid matrix describes the benign pleomorphic adenoma, not mucoepidermoid carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A benign oncocytic tumor with lymphoid stroma describes Warthin tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Barrett esophagus gives rise to esophageal adenocarcinoma, not a salivary gland malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV-driven nonkeratinizing carcinoma describes oropharyngeal SCC, not mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman underwent enucleation of a benign parotid mixed tumor several years ago and now returns with a recurrent mass at the same site; biopsy shows areas of malignant transformation. Which salivary gland tumor is best known for this behavior of local recurrence and potential malignant transformation?

explanation.summary: Pleomorphic adenoma can recur after resection and undergo malignant transformation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pleomorphic adenoma, though benign, carries a risk of local recurrence (especially after incomplete excision) and can undergo malignant transformation (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Warthin tumor is benign and rarely recurs or transforms; it is smoking-associated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is already a malignancy, not a benign tumor that transforms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is malignant from the outset and known for perineural invasion, not benign-to-malignant transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Basal cell adenoma is a rare benign tumor not characterized by this classic recurrence/transformation behavior.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: An immunohistochemical stain is ordered on an oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma to determine whether it is human papillomavirus-associated. Which marker, when positive, indicates HPV involvement?

explanation.summary: p16 positivity is the immunohistochemical surrogate marker for HPV in oropharyngeal SCC.
explanation.whyCorrect: p16 overexpression is used as a marker of high-risk HPV involvement in oropharyngeal SCC; such tumors are typically nonkeratinizing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CEA is a nonspecific marker for various adenocarcinomas, not an HPV surrogate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD117 (c-KIT) is used in GISTs and some salivary tumors, not to indicate HPV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromogranin is a neuroendocrine marker, unrelated to HPV status.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Synaptophysin is a neuroendocrine marker, not a marker of HPV involvement.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A pathologist notes that esophageal cancers frequently show early lymph node involvement compared with cancers elsewhere in the gut. Which anatomic feature of the esophagus best explains this tendency?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The esophagus has an unusually thick serosa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Esophageal lymphatics lie within the lamina propria rather than below the muscularis mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Esophageal tumors are always high grade

choices.label: E
choices.text: The esophagus lacks any submucosal layer

explanation.summary: Esophageal lymphatics sit in the lamina propria, permitting early nodal spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike the rest of the gut, where lymphatics lie below the muscularis mucosa, esophageal lymphatics are located in the lamina propria. Tumor cells therefore reach lymphatics at an earlier stage, promoting early lymph node metastasis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no such lymphangiogenic hormone mechanism; the explanation is anatomic lymphatic location.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The esophagus lacks a serosa over most of its length, which aids spread but is not the lymphatic explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grade varies among esophageal tumors and does not explain the anatomic pattern of early nodal spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The esophagus does have a submucosa; the key point is the superficial location of lymphatics in the lamina propria.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with fatigue, dysphagia, glossitis, and koilonychia. Labs show microcytic anemia, and a barium swallow reveals a cervical esophageal web. This constellation increases her risk for which esophageal malignancy?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the upper esophagus

explanation.summary: Plummer-Vinson syndrome (iron-deficiency anemia, dysphagia, esophageal webs) predisposes to esophageal SCC.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is Plummer-Vinson syndrome, a recognized risk factor for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, which arises in the upper two thirds of the esophagus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Distal adenocarcinoma is associated with Barrett esophagus/GERD, not Plummer-Vinson syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is a salivary gland tumor, not the esophageal cancer linked to esophageal webs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Small cell carcinoma of the esophagus is rare and not the Plummer-Vinson-associated malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GIST is a mesenchymal tumor unrelated to Plummer-Vinson syndrome.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A comparison is made between HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC and non-HPV oral cavity SCC. Which of the following features is most characteristic of the HPV-associated tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Median age older than 61 years with keratinizing histology

choices.label: B
choices.text: Large primary tumor with prominent hoarseness and dysphagia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Strong association with chewing tobacco of the buccal mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arises in the ventral tongue and floor of mouth from alcohol use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presents as an asymptomatic neck mass with a small primary and nonkeratinizing p16-positive histology

explanation.summary: HPV-associated SCC presents as an asymptomatic neck mass with a small primary and nonkeratinizing p16-positive histology.
explanation.whyCorrect: HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC (tonsils, base of tongue) typically presents with an asymptomatic neck mass and cervical lymphadenopathy from a small primary; it is nonkeratinizing and p16 positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Older age (median 61) with keratinizing histology describes the non-HPV, tobacco/alcohol-related tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Large primary tumors with hoarseness and dysphagia characterize non-HPV keratinizing SCC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chewing tobacco of the buccal mucosa drives non-HPV oral cavity SCC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ventral tongue and floor-of-mouth tumors from alcohol describe the non-HPV oral cavity subtype.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with recurrent, metastatic oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma has progressed after surgery and chemotherapy. His oncologist adds an immune checkpoint inhibitor. Which of the following agents is a PD-1 inhibitor used for advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma?

explanation.summary: Pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, is used as immunotherapy for advanced oral/head and neck SCC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pembrolizumab is a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor used as immunotherapy in advanced or recurrent/metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor for acid suppression, not an immunotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cisplatin is a cytotoxic chemotherapy agent, not a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trastuzumab is an anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody used in HER2-positive cancers, not a PD-1 inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody used in B-cell lymphomas, not a PD-1 inhibitor for SCC.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has a slow-growing parotid mass. Resection shows a tumor with cribriform 'Swiss cheese' nests of cells and prominent perineural invasion, and he reports facial numbness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Cribriform nests with perineural invasion and facial numbness point to adenoid cystic carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a salivary gland malignancy classically showing cribriform ('Swiss cheese') architecture and a strong tendency for perineural invasion, which can cause facial pain or numbness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Warthin tumor is benign with oncocytic epithelium over lymphoid stroma and no perineural invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pleomorphic adenoma is benign with a chondromyxoid matrix and does not classically invade nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratinocytes and keratinization, not cribriform gland nests.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Esophageal adenocarcinoma arises in the distal esophagus from Barrett metaplasia, not the parotid.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: During evaluation of a suspected oral cavity neoplasm, the clinician wants to visualize the pharynx and hypopharynx directly as part of the workup before biopsy. Which of the following is the most appropriate step?

explanation.summary: Flexible laryngoscopy is used to directly visualize the pharynx during oral cavity neoplasm workup.
explanation.whyCorrect: Workup of a suspected oral cavity neoplasm includes physical exam of the oral cavity, flexible laryngoscopy to visualize the pharynx, examination of neck nodal drainage, staging CT, and tissue biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colonoscopy evaluates the colon and is irrelevant to a head and neck neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Capsule endoscopy images the small bowel, not the pharynx.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bronchoscopy evaluates the tracheobronchial tree, not the primary approach to visualize the pharynx here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ERCP evaluates the biliary and pancreatic ducts, unrelated to oral cavity neoplasm workup.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: A researcher summarizes the epidemiology of head and neck cancers for a lecture. Approximately what proportion of head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas, and how does this cancer rank globally?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 50%, and it is the most common neoplasm worldwide

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 70%, and it is the second most common neoplasm worldwide

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 30%, and it is a rare neoplasm worldwide

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 95%, and it is the sixth most common neoplasm worldwide

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 10%, and it is the tenth most common neoplasm worldwide

explanation.summary: SCC accounts for ~95% of head and neck cancers and is the sixth most common neoplasm worldwide.
explanation.whyCorrect: Approximately 95% of head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas, and head and neck SCC is the sixth most common neoplasm in the world.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The proportion is about 95%, not 50%, and it is the sixth most common, not the single most common, neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The figure is about 95%, not 70%, and it ranks sixth, not second.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SCC is far more common than 30% and is not a rare neoplasm; it accounts for ~95% of head and neck cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It represents about 95%, not 10%, of head and neck cancers, and ranks sixth globally.

questions.topicName: Oral, Salivary Gland, and Esophageal Neoplasms
questions.stem: An attending contrasts the two main histologic types of esophageal cancer for students. Which of the following pairings of location and predominant setting is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenocarcinoma in the upper two thirds; SCC in the distal third

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both types arise only at the gastroesophageal junction

choices.label: C
choices.text: SCC arises from Barrett esophagus; adenocarcinoma from smoking

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adenocarcinoma is the most common type worldwide; SCC is most common in the Western world

choices.label: E
choices.text: SCC in the upper two thirds and most common worldwide; adenocarcinoma in the distal third and most common in the Western world

explanation.summary: SCC occupies the upper two thirds and leads worldwide; adenocarcinoma occupies the distal third and leads in the West.
explanation.whyCorrect: Esophageal SCC arises in the upper two thirds and is the most common type worldwide, whereas adenocarcinoma arises in the distal third from Barrett esophagus and is the most common type in the Western world.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the locations: adenocarcinoma is distal and SCC is in the upper two thirds.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither type is confined to the gastroesophageal junction; they occupy different esophageal regions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the associations: adenocarcinoma arises from Barrett esophagus, and SCC is linked to smoking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses global patterns: SCC predominates worldwide, and adenocarcinoma predominates in the Western world.
